title: ImageNet and AlexNet (2012)
text:
CHAPTER 16. DEEP LEARNING
SECTION 16.2. IMAGENET AND ALEXNET (2012)

The single event most often cited as the start of the deep learning era happened in autumn 2012, at a computer vision competition. A convolutional neural network from Geoffrey Hinton's group in Toronto, later called AlexNet after its first author Alex Krizhevsky, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a top-5 error rate of 15.3 percent, against about 26 percent for the runner-up. Within two or three years almost the whole field of computer vision had switched to deep networks, and companies began investing heavily in the technology. AlexNet's success came from three ingredients arriving together: a large labeled dataset, GPU computing, and a few technical improvements to old architectures. This section explains each.

1. Data: the creation of ImageNet

Before ImageNet, computer vision datasets were small: PASCAL VOC had 20 object categories and thousands of images; Caltech-101 had 101 categories. Models trained on them could not learn the variety of the visual world, and evaluation on them was noisy.

Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton (she moved to Stanford in 2009), began working on the idea for ImageNet in 2006. She wanted to expand the data available to train algorithms rather than only improve the algorithms, at a time when most research focused on models. The dataset was organized by WordNet, a lexical database of English that groups nouns into hierarchical sets of synonyms ("synsets"); ImageNet started from roughly 22,000 noun categories. Candidate images were collected from internet search engines, and humans verified which images actually showed each category.

The labeling scale was a problem. By one estimate in Wikipedia's account, at a rate of about 2 images per second, labeling would take about 19 human-years of continuous work. The team used Amazon Mechanical Turk, an online marketplace for small paid tasks, to distribute the verification to thousands of workers, with several votes per image to control quality. Labeling ran from July 2008 to April 2010. The database was first presented as a poster at the 2009 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) by Jia Deng, Wei Dong, Richard Socher, Li-Jia Li, Kai Li and Li Fei-Fei, and the project was initially met with skepticism. ImageNet eventually contained over 14 million labeled images in about 22,000 categories.

2. The challenge (ILSVRC)

The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge started in 2010. Its classification task used a trimmed subset: 1,000 categories (including 90 of the 120 dog breeds in the full schema, which made fine-grained classification part of the test), about 1.2 million training images, and 50,000 validation and 100,000 test images.

Metric: top-5 error. The model outputs five guesses per image; it is correct if the true label is among them. This tolerates ambiguous images (a picture may contain several objects).

Early winners used hand-designed features and linear classifiers: in 2010 and 2011 the winners were SVM-based systems using features such as SIFT and Fisher vectors (Section 14.2), with the 2011 winner at a top-5 error of about 25 percent. Progress was incremental.

3. AlexNet

Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Hinton entered ILSVRC 2012 as team "SuperVision" and described their network in "ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks" at the NIPS 2012 conference (later reprinted in Communications of the ACM, 2017). The official results list SuperVision's best entry at a top-5 test error of 0.153 (15.3 percent), using extra training data from the ImageNet Fall 2011 release; their entry without extra data reached about 16.4 percent. The second-best team, ISI (University of Tokyo), reached about 26.2 percent with Fisher vector features and linear classifiers. A margin of more than 10 percentage points, in a field used to improvements of one or two, was a shock.

Architecture. AlexNet was a direct descendant of LeNet (Section 13.3), but much larger:

    input: 224 x 224 x 3 RGB image (crops of 256 x 256 images)
    conv1: 96 kernels of 11 x 11, stride 4, ReLU, then local response normalization and max pooling
    conv2: 256 kernels of 5 x 5, ReLU, normalization, max pooling
    conv3: 384 kernels of 3 x 3, ReLU
    conv4: 384 kernels of 3 x 3, ReLU
    conv5: 256 kernels of 3 x 3, ReLU, max pooling
    fc6:   4096 units, ReLU, dropout
    fc7:   4096 units, ReLU, dropout
    fc8:   1000 units, softmax

about 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons. Most parameters are in the fully connected layers: fc6 alone connects a 6 x 6 x 256 = 9,216-dimensional input to 4,096 units, about 37.7 million weights. The convolutional layers have far fewer parameters but do most of the computation.

The softmax output turns 1,000 scores z_k into probabilities

    p_k = exp(z_k) / sum_j exp(z_j)

trained with the cross-entropy loss -log p_correct (Section 13.1).

4. The technical ingredients

ReLU. AlexNet used rectified linear units, f(z) = max(0, z), instead of tanh or sigmoid. ReLU does not saturate for positive inputs, so its gradient is 1 there, and it is cheap to compute. The paper reported that a four-layer convolutional network with ReLUs reached 25 percent training error on the CIFAR-10 dataset several times faster than the same network with tanh units. (ReLU-like units had been used before, for example by Fukushima and in work by Vinod Nair and Hinton in 2010 and Xavier Glorot, Antoine Bordes and Bengio in 2011.)

Dropout. In the two large fully connected layers, each unit's output was set to zero with probability 0.5 during training (and outputs were scaled at test time). This prevents units from relying on specific other units ("co-adaptation") and acts like training a huge ensemble of thinned networks that share weights. It greatly reduced overfitting (Section 16.3).

Data augmentation. To enlarge the effective training set, they trained on random 224 x 224 crops of the 256 x 256 images and their horizontal mirror images, and perturbed the RGB colors along their principal components (simulating lighting changes). At test time they averaged predictions over ten crops (four corners and center, plus their mirrors).

GPUs. The network was trained with GPU code Krizhevsky had written ("cuda-convnet"). Because the model did not fit in the 3 GB memory of a single Nvidia GTX 580, it was split across two GPUs, with half of the kernels of each layer on each GPU and communication only at certain layers. Training took about five to six days for 90 passes (epochs) over the 1.2 million images. According to the commonly told story, the GPUs were in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house.

Optimization. Stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9, batch size 128, weight decay 0.0005 (L2 regularization), and a learning rate of 0.01 divided by 10 when validation error stopped improving.

Overlapping pooling and local response normalization were also used; later networks dropped local response normalization as unnecessary.

None of these was a fundamental new idea in isolation. The breakthrough was making them all work together at a scale, enabled by GPUs and ImageNet, that nobody had tried.

5. What the network learned

The first-layer kernels learned oriented edge detectors at various frequencies and color-blob detectors, much like Gabor filters and the simple cells of Hubel and Wiesel (Section 13.3). Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus (2013-2014) developed visualization methods showing that deeper layers respond to textures, then object parts (eyes, wheels), then whole objects. The 4,096-dimensional activations of the last hidden layer turned out to be excellent general image descriptors: images with similar activations were semantically similar even when their pixels differed greatly. Using such pretrained features for other tasks (transfer learning) quickly beat hand-designed features on many vision problems (for example, DeCAF and Razavian and colleagues' "CNN features off-the-shelf," both 2013-2014).

6. The aftermath

Progress on ILSVRC after 2012 was rapid:

  - 2013: ZFNet (Zeiler and Fergus), a refined AlexNet, won with lower error.
  - 2014: VGG networks (Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman, Oxford), using stacks of small 3 x 3 convolutions with 16-19 layers, and GoogLeNet (Christian Szegedy and colleagues at Google), with "inception" modules, reached top-5 errors of roughly 7 percent.
  - 2015: Residual networks (ResNets; Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun, Microsoft Research) with 152 layers reached about 3.6 percent, below the roughly 5 percent error estimated for a trained human annotator in a study by Andrej Karpathy (Section 16.3).
  - 2017: the final ILSVRC classification winner (Squeeze-and-Excitation networks) reached about 2.3 percent; with most teams above 95 percent accuracy, the challenge ended.

The same networks were adapted for object detection (R-CNN, 2014, and successors such as Faster R-CNN and YOLO), segmentation and pose estimation. In industry, Google acquired DNNresearch, the company founded by Hinton, Krizhevsky and Sutskever, in 2013 (commonly reported as early 2013, following an auction among several companies), and Facebook, Microsoft, Baidu and others built deep learning groups. Nvidia began to position its GPUs for AI.

Criticism and limits also became clearer. ImageNet labels contain errors and ambiguities (studies have estimated that a noticeable fraction of validation labels, around 10 percent by some estimates, are ambiguous or wrong). The person categories in the full ImageNet contained offensive and biased labels, which led the dataset's maintainers to filter many of the person categories around 2019-2020, a reminder that datasets embed the choices and biases of their makers. Benchmark accuracy also proved fragile: networks could be fooled by tiny "adversarial" perturbations (Szegedy and colleagues, 2013) and often performed worse on newly collected test sets from the same distribution.

7. Why 2012?

The elements had existed separately: CNNs since 1989, backpropagation since the 1970s-1980s, GPUs for neural networks since 2004-2006, large datasets since 2009. AlexNet combined them. The lesson the field drew, sometimes called the "bitter lesson" (a 2019 essay by Richard Sutton), was that general methods that scale with computation and data tend to beat methods built on human-designed knowledge, a reversal of the expert systems philosophy (Chapter 12). That lesson drove the scaling of models through the 2010s and 2020s (Chapter 19).

8. For a mechatronics engineer

AlexNet-era methods are now routine tools:

  - Transfer learning: start from a network pretrained on ImageNet (or a larger dataset) and fine-tune it on a few hundred or thousand labeled images of your parts, defects or scenes. This is usually far better than training from scratch on small data.
  - Data augmentation: crops, flips, rotations, brightness changes; choose augmentations that match real variation in your camera setup (for example, no horizontal flips if left and right orientation matters).
  - Efficient architectures for embedded use (MobileNet, EfficientNet and others) are the descendants of AlexNet optimized for phones and edge devices.
  - Evaluate on images from the actual deployment conditions; benchmark accuracy does not guarantee robustness to new lighting, cameras or part variants.

9. Summary

  - ImageNet (Fei-Fei Li and colleagues; idea from 2006, CVPR 2009 poster, labeling via Amazon Mechanical Turk 2008-2010) eventually had over 14 million images in about 22,000 WordNet categories.
  - ILSVRC (from 2010) used 1,000 classes and about 1.2 million training images; early winners used SVMs on hand-designed features (about 25 percent top-5 error in 2011).
  - AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton; NIPS 2012) had 5 convolutional and 3 fully connected layers, about 60 million parameters, and reached 15.3 percent top-5 error versus about 26.2 percent for the runner-up.
  - Key ingredients: ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, and training on two GTX 580 GPUs for five to six days.
  - Rapid progress followed (VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet), with top-5 error falling to a few percent by 2015-2017; deep learning spread through vision and industry.
